newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia rebels give conditional OK to peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Colombia rebels give conditional OK to peace talks.

text.p: Colombia's oldest and largest guerrilla army is prepared to take part in government-backed peace talks but will not negotiate with illegal right-wing death squads, one of its top leaders said on Sunday.

Raul Reyes, member of the seven-man national secretariat of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), told the NTC TV news program by telephone from Costa Rica: "The FARC is prepared to talk to the government and components of the state but not to (paramilitary) groups outside the law."
"We would also be ready to talk to the military because they are part of the problem and should be there," he added.

Recently-appointed Defense Minister Gilberto Echeverri raised the possibility 10 days ago of a fresh peace process including the government, civic groups, the military and illegal armed groups of the left and right.
President Ernesto Samper followed up by announcing he would call a "peace summit" after Easter to look at possible ways of ending Colombia's three-decade-old guerrilla uprising.
No firm proposal has been made on the exact format a new peace process would follow.

The FARC has always said the quickest way to end its guerrilla war is through negotiations with the government but it has insisted in the past that talks would have to address a wide range of social, political and economic issues.

In the NTC interview, Reyes also said the FARC would insist on the demilitarization of vast swathes of eastern Meta province, the rebel force's traditional power base, before peace talks could begin. The military rejected a guerrilla proposal that it pull out of the area in 1995, saying it had the constitutional obligation to safeguard national security.

In comments to reporters on Sunday, Gen. Harold Bedoya, the head of Colombia's armed forces, reacted coolly to the idea of peace talks, saying: "Anything that's constitutional we will do and anything that is not we will not do."
Previous attempts to hammer out a peace deal with the FARC, set up as a pro-Soviet force in 1964, have failed.

In a separate development, at least 10 FARC rebels have been killed in firefights with the army in the violence-torn, northwest banana-growing region of Uraba since Thursday, regional commander Gen. Rito Alejo del Rio said on Sunday.
The latest clash took place on Sunday afternoon near the town of Riosucio, in which one guerrilla was shot dead and quantities of explosives were seized, Del Rio said.
